title: For restaurants Covid-19 was a crisis – pandemic loans are proving a disaster
desc:
Low-interest loans kept many eateries afloat. But the industry never recovered enough for them to repay the debt

For almost 20 years, Jai Mazumdar has served vegetarian curries, samosas, gulab jamun and other Indian delicacies at Spice N Curry, a cafe and grocery nestled inside a modest strip mall near Florida International University (FIU) in Miami. When the Covid-19 pandemic devastated his business, as it did with so many restaurants, Mazumdar took out a $370,000 economic injury disaster loan (EIDL) from the federal government in early 2021.

At the time, it provided a desperately needed lifeline. He was confident that once business returned to normal he could begin repaying the 30-year loan, which came with a low 3.75% interest rate and a 30-month deferment period. But when his business didn’t recover, the disaster loan turned out to be a disaster of its own.

title: Will Trump’s economy sink Republicans in the US midterm elections? Our reporters answered your questions
desc:
The high cost of living has Americans angrier than ever. Guardian reporters answered your questions about the US economy ahead of November

  • Sign up for the Stakes newsletter for more midterms coverage

  • Send us your questions on Trump’s immigration agenda ahead of the midterms

LucccA asks: Why are labor unions in the US still not as well-organized compared to the rest of the world? I know there was a push against them in the past—does that still have an effect today? Also, why are there so many right-leaning unions in the US?

Michael: A lot of reasons. The US has low union density compared to other wealthy nations, currently at 10.0%, and that has been on a precipitous decline for the past few decades for a variety of reasons that include anti-union and union busting campaigns, outdated labor laws where employers often retaliate for union organizing or delay bargaining for years, as we are seeing with Starbucks, where there is no union contract after nearly five years since the first store won its union election in December 2021.Right to work laws in the US also undermine labor unions and starve them of resources. To the extent that there are right leaning labor unions in the US, they typically are law enforcement unions that consistently endorse and back Republican candidates despite the Republican Party in the US opposing collective bargaining. Some unions like the Teamsters have been making efforts to get Republicans to support legislation and in turn receive endorsements from the union, and this has shown up this election cycle with the Teamsters endorsing Republicans like Congressman Max Miller or Kansas Senator Roger Marshall, who are both facing very competitive re-election battles.

Heather: There’s a bunch of ideas floating around on cutting costs for groceries, healthcare and energy bills. A key thing Democrats are promising if they regain power in Congress is to wrestle back authority on trade and repeal Trump’s tariffs, which would lower what it costs compaines to import. A second is to advance a vote to stop the war in Iran, which could calm fuel prices. If Democrats retake the Senate, expect Elizabeth Warren to become chair of the powerful banking committe, and push forward some curbs on private equity investments. And Democrats have been coalescing around more government funding for childcare, a notable move to the left in recent years. Hakeem Jeffries, who will be House Speaker if Democrats win there, is promising to reinstate ACA tax cuts and roll back Medicaid cuts, but the party is divided on Medicare For All, with DSA candidates making promises on the campaign trail and more centrist Dems being pretty quiet.

Republicans running for Congress have been talking a lot about ways to lower gas prices, especially suspending the fuel tax, and shaving utility bills by making tech companies and other big users pay more. Some have promised to curb Trump’s tariffs, including Michigan’s Mike Rogers, and others are proposing suspending data center building after public backlash.

title: SpaceX Earnings Preview: Equity Sees $125 Billion, Credit Sees 83 Cents
desc:
SpaceX Earnings Preview: Equity Sees $125 Billion, Credit Sees 83 Cents

Today after the close, SpaceX (SPCX) reports its second quarter as a public company, a day ahead of Tesla and (as Deutsche Bank puts it) "surprisingly early." The first one did not go well: the stock slid despite a big revenue beat and closed down 14% the next day, wiping out some $225 billion in market value.

This time, the sellside is mostly looking past the quarter and straight at 2027. Nobody more so than Deutsche Bank's Edison Yu, who in his preview note "Compute-driven state of mind" (available to pro subs) lifts his 2027 forecasts to $125 billion in revenue and $84 billion in EBITDA, materially above consensus of $108 billion and $65 billion. The catch, which Yu flags himself, is that those numbers are "underpinned by > $200bn in capex."

And that's where the other half of the SpaceX story comes in. While equity analysts debate how high 2027 can go, the company's 6.65% notes due 2056 just slumped to a lifetime low of 83.3 cents on the dollar, down from 98.83 at issue in June, and SpaceX's five-year CDS spreads blew out to a record high earlier this month.

In other words, the stock market is pricing the upside, and the bond market is pricing the bill.

The Quarter: In Line, With "Potential Upside In Profitability"

Start with the near term. Deutsche expects an in-line print, "with potential upside in profitability." Yu models Q3 revenue of $12.6 billion (+127% YoY), a gross margin of around 59% and EBITDA of over $6.6 billion. The engine is AI, which "is benefiting from a full-quarter contribution from cloud hosting, boosting revenue by almost 3x sequentially to ~$6bn." AI solutions & infrastructure alone is expected to jump from $2.2 billion in Q2 to $6.0 billion, which means the AI segment would account for just over half of total revenue at the business formerly known as a rocket company.

Elsewhere, consumer broadband subscribers should end the quarter at 13.5 million (vs. 12.0 million in Q2), while ARPU slides another $2 to $64, giving connectivity revenue of nearly $5 billion, up 60% YoY. The Space segment, the one in the company's name, is expected to shrink 22% YoY on twelve external Falcon 9 launches. As for the cash, Yu forecasts $19 billion in capex "mainly directed at AI compute," taking capacity to 1.8GW, and leading to free cash flow burn of $14 billion, in one quarter.

Here is the full breakdown vs. consensus:

Note that Deutsche is slightly below the Street on Q3 revenue ($12.63 billion vs. $12.89 billion) and broadband subs (13.5 million vs. 14.2 million), but slightly above on EBITDA margin (52.6% vs. 51.4%). Options are pricing a move of about 7.8% in either direction, which is a bit more than half of what the stock actually did after Q2.

How High Can 2027 Go?

This is where Deutsche gets interesting. In Yu's view, "the largest swing factor in respect to forecasts will be compute deployment." Management is targeting more than 2GW exiting 4Q26, which DB thinks is "doable," and then 5-10GW exiting 2027. DB models toward the low end, at about 6GW, and lays out a line of sight into 5-7GW of power over the next couple of years: 1.9GW of Doosan turbines, 1.2GW from the Southaven plant's 41 turbines, 0.7-1.1GW from the APR acquisition, 900MW or more leased through the Stateline JV, plus the TVA grid supply and backup turbines at Colossus 1 and up to another gigawatt "from other sources." (We assume SpaceX will need all of it to keep the Nvidia chips it is borrowing to buy switched on.)

Put it together, and the bank's math says the neocloud business alone can generate $70-90 billion of revenue in 2027, "depending on timing and pricing dynamics." For context, SpaceX's entire 2025 revenue was $18.7 billion. And the result is a 2027 forecast that is now 16% above consensus on revenue and 29% above on EBITDA:

Deutsche isn't even the most aggressive on compute. Goldman's Eric Sheridan, in his own SpaceX Q3'26 preview earlier this month (also available to pro subs), forecasts SpaceX scaling to ~2.4GW of AI compute by year-end, ~7.0GW by the end of 2027 and ~10.6GW by the end of 2028:

Goldman models $85.5 billion in 2027 AI solutions & infrastructure revenue, of which $45.5 billion comes from hosting deals on just ~1GW of contracted capacity. As we noted when we dug through Goldman's neocloud rate card, most of those hosting deals are "90-day cancellable on both sides." Which is probably worth keeping in mind when somebody extrapolates them to 2029.

Speaking of extrapolating, Musk himself already raised the bar on the Q2 call:

Musk reiterates expectation of $100 billion ARR by the end of this year (10x the June ARR), and now sees SpaceX seeing $1 trillion in revenue by 2030, and "non zero chance" of getting there in 2029. Some context: the average analyst estimate (30 of 39 sellside analysts are Buy on SPCX) for 2029 revenue is $208 billion

— zerohedge (@zerohedge) August 4, 2026

Evercore's Kutgun Maral, for one, expects an annual run rate of $104 billion by year-end and 2.3GW of compute (vs. the Street's 2.2GW), and raised his target to $270. Deutsche keeps its Buy and $235 target, vs. Friday's close of $146.03.

The $200 Billion Footnote

Here is the full set of DB's estimate changes. Look at the bottom line of each block:

Deutsche raised 2027 revenue by $10 billion, and 2027 capex by $22 billion, to $207 billion, and 2028 capex by $40 billion to $230 billion. And while 2028 revenue barely moves ($200 billion vs. $198 billion), 2028 EPS actually dips, because, as Yu admits, "there is concern by investors that pricing could normalize in 2028-29." The bank now assumes $/GW pricing "declines by 25% to about $30bn in 2028." In other words, the compute gets more expensive to build exactly when it gets cheaper to rent.

Line up DB's own EBITDA against DB's own capex, and the problem becomes obvious:

Napkin math: under Deutsche's bullish model, capex exceeds EBITDA by about $47 billion this year, $124 billion in 2027 and $81 billion in 2028, or roughly $250 billion across three years. SpaceX ended Q2 with $100 billion in cash and marketable securities, and DB expects about $13.5 billion of that to have been burned in Q3 alone. Which means the 2027 gap by itself is bigger than the cash pile... and that gap has to be filled by someone.

That someone, of course, is the bond market.

Meanwhile, In Credit...

Regular readers will recall that SpaceX slammed head first into the bond market less than two weeks after its record $86 billion IPO, selling $25 billion of investment grade bonds which were, depending on who you asked, "4x oversubscribed." Bondholders have been underwater pretty much since the break, and on Monday the 6.65% notes of 2056 hit a new all-time low of 83.345:

At that price, the 30-year paper of a BBB-rated company that is supposedly about to post $84 billion in EBITDA yields roughly 8.1%, which is the kind of number one usually associates with the junk bond market (as we put it back in August, "SPCX bonds skeptical about the $1 trillion in revenue"). The 5.875% notes due 2036 tell the same story: per Trace, their spread was 193bps earlier this month, vs. 140bps when they were sold in June.

What changed? The record chip-collateralized loan. On Oct 6, the FT reported that SpaceX wants to raise another $40 billion, about $10 billion in bank loans and $30 billion of IG debt, in a deal led by Apollo, to pay for Nvidia chips. Add the $25 billion from June, and SpaceX will have borrowed (or tried to borrow) $65 billion since June, on top of the $38.4 billion in debt it reported as of June 30. The next day, five-year CDS jumped as much as 16.7bps to about 197.6bps, the highest since the swaps started actively trading in June (when they were around 110bps):

Of course, we covered it at the time:

Barclays' credit analysts, led by Andrew Keches, argued that an SPV structure might be good for SpaceX in the long run by reducing the amount of debt at the parent company, but warned that in the near term the coming supply could put pressure on the company's existing bonds.

Well, they were right about the near term: less than two weeks later, the bonds are 1.4 points lower than where they were on Oct 7, and DB's revised capex forecast suggests $40 billion won't be the last ask. Or as Coherence Credit's Sal Naro told Bloomberg, speaking of AI debt in general: "This is unprecedented debt supply with no real ending in sight."

None of this will surprise those who have been reading us since last October, when we first warned that AI had quietly become a debt bubble too, and that the debt would sooner or later have to compete with everyone else (including Uncle Sam) for the same duration buyers. SpaceX, which Musk said in December had been cash-flow positive for years and didn't really need anyone's money, is now one of the biggest borrowers in that line.

What To Watch Today After The Close

Deutsche's own list of "other areas of focus" is a good checklist:

  • AI: neocloud pricing and new contracts, the Cursor contribution, Grok Bot adoption, and the data center capex outlook (read: any hint that 2027 capex starts with a "2").
  • Launch: timing of the next few launches after Flight 14; Flight 15 looks set for mid-/late November, though DB doesn't expect a second-stage catch.
  • Connectivity: after the $8 billion Grain spectrum deal, "additional color on management's next move(s) in the US (build vs. buy)," which is something the wireless carriers will be listening to closely.
  • Tesla merger: DB sees the timing as "mainly a function of valuation differentials and politics (may want to avoid a potential Democrat-led administration taking over post Trump)."

To that we'd add one more: anything on financing. Specifically, whether the $40 billion Apollo deal is done, how much of it sits in an SPV, and how much more is coming. And, after today's pledge of a SpaceX share to "every kid in America," maybe also how many shares that is.

Who Blinks First?

Deutsche's long-term thesis (as well as everyone else's for that matter) is straightforward: "the endgame is to build and possess the greatest amount of compute at the lowest cost on the ground and eventually in orbit," which should eventually let SpaceX "deliver leading intelligence/inference capabilities which we think investors generally are still quite skeptical about." Yu also concedes that "the stock has increasingly traded more in line with the AI cohort as opposed to Space." Morgan Stanley's Adam Jonas, who has become the bank's resident in house SpaceX cheerleader and now covers only this company, thinks SpaceX "looks unusually cheap" on the forward (duh), recently described the skepticism even more vividly: asked who owned the stock, out of 40 clients "not a single hand went up."

So who is right: the equity analysts who see 2027 EBITDA nearly 30% above consensus, or the bondholders who are demanding 8% for 30 years? Probably both, in their own way.

The upside case is real, but every dollar of DB's 2027 EBITDA comes with roughly two and a half dollars of capex attached, and that capex will be funded by the same creditors who just marked the 2056s to 83. If today's call brings a higher capex number and no clarity on financing, we suspect the bond market will be the one setting the tone, just as it did after Q2. Then again, Musk has never been shy about telling bears that he "tried to warn them," and as of Friday's close the stock was still 8% above its $135 IPO price. The bonds, meanwhile, are almost 16% below theirs.

Much more in the full Deutsche Bank "Compute-driven state of mind" note and Goldman's "SpaceX Q3'26 preview," both available to pro subs.

The expansion follows JPMorgan’s November 2025 rollout of JPM Coin on Base, an Ethereum layer-2 network built by cryptocurrency exchange Coinbase.

At the time, JPMorgan said it planned to support additional public blockchains. In January, JPMorgan announced plans to bring JPM Coin to the Canton Network.

title: Florida Issues Arrest Warrant For Former Cuban Leader Raul Castro
desc:
Florida Issues Arrest Warrant For Former Cuban Leader Raul Castro

Authored by Troy Myers via The Epoch Times,

Florida is seeking to arrest former Cuban leader Raúl Castro over his alleged role in a conspiracy to shoot down and murder three U.S. citizens and one lawful resident aboard two civilian aircraft more than 30 years ago.

The state arrest warrant was announced Monday by Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier, who accused Castro of having spies embedded in America to help carry out the shooting down of two unarmed planes operated by Brothers to the Rescue, a humanitarian organization that promotes Cubans' efforts against the country's long-standing communist regime.

The former Cuban leader, now in his mid-90s, is charged with one count of conspiracy to commit first-degree murder and also faces a parallel, federal indictment by the Department of Justice, announced May 20.

"Raúl Castro ordered the murder of four Floridians in cold blood, and Florida will never stop pursuing accountability for that communist conspiracy," Uthmeier said in a news release. "The Castro regime's spies operated in our communities, fed intelligence to Havana, and helped put civilian pilots in the crosshairs of Cuban MiGs."

The four victims in the planes shot down on Feb. 24, 1996, were Carlos Costa, Pablo Morales, Mario de la Peña, and Armando Alejandre Jr.

According to the affidavit, Castro, who was the minister of Cuba's Revolutionary Armed Forces and first vice president at the time of the incident, was the final decider in authorizing the attack, giving senior military officials an order to "shoot them down at sea when they show up, and those who have the authority are not to consult anyone."

Cuban spies operating in South Florida's Miami-Dade and Monroe Counties infiltrated the Brothers to the Rescue organization and reported their flight plans back to Cuban leaders, the news release said.

On the day of the attack, three unarmed Brothers to the Rescue aircraft departed the Opa-Locka Airport in Miami-Dade County. Once they crossed the 24th latitude line, while still outside the island-nation's territory, Cuban MiGs destroyed two of the civilian Cessnas with missiles, killing the four onboard.

"For thirty years, their families and our Cuban American community have carried this profound loss and refused to let the pursuit of justice fade," Miami-Dade Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz said in the news release. "Today's action sends a clear message: the passage of time does not diminish the value of these lives or our responsibility to pursue accountability."

The news release added that the aircraft were traveling away from Cuba and received no warning before the attack.

Elements of the alleged criminal conspiracy, like the gathering of intel by stateside Cuban spies, occurred in Miami-Dade and Monroe Counties. Chief Judge Ariana Fajardo Orshan of the 11th Judicial Circuit, which encompasses Miami-Dade, signed the arrest warrant.

Florida's Office of Statewide Prosecution has assumed jurisdiction of the ongoing investigation, Uthmeier said, and additional charges against Castro are possible.

"Under President [Donald] Trump's administration, we're committed to pursuing every lawful, prosecutable avenue to bring accountability, including parallel federal and state prosecutions," U.S. Attorney Jason Quiñones said in the news release.

Florida's arrest warrant against Castro joins the United States' increasing pressure campaign against Cuba's brutal communist rule, as Trump administration officials have long stated their intentions of wanting regime change on the island nation.

On Aug. 6, the State Department announced sanctions against Cuba's military.

More recently, Trump took the stage at the United Nations on Sept. 22 and called Cuba a failed state, adding that "freedom will be coming" to the island. The Cuban delegation walked out.

A week after that speech, Trump told reporters at the White House that he believed the United States and Cuba could reach an agreement, and American military action would not be necessary.

Prior to that comment, the president hinted in June that a potential Cuba operation could mirror the Caracas, Venezuela, raid on Jan. 3 to apprehend then-Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores, both of whom are in custody in New York and pleading not guilty to a number of charges.

Cuban Americans told The Epoch Times they were hopeful for U.S. military action against their home country following the overnight operation in Caracas.

They also reacted with glee over the U.S. indictment against Castro in May.

Alina Fernández Revuelta, the daughter of Fidel Castro, welcomed the charges against her uncle.

"The charges increase pressure on a regime untouchable for decades," she told The Epoch Times in a text message. "Coming from a family directly connected to that history, you understand the weight of this moment in a different way."

Baruah lowered his 12-month price target to $330 from $370, nearly in line with Bloomberg-tracked analyst forecasts of around $334. The new target implies roughly 4% downside from the $343 share price cited in the note.

Baruah explained the reason for the rating downgrade:

We're downgrading AAPL to Hold from Buy and lowering our PT to $330 from $370 on new iPhone data from Loop Capital Supply Chain Analyst John Donovan (Latest AAPL ASP Tracker & Build Analysis – Reported Cuts Not True – Yet?) as our "normalized" EPS is reduced to $11.00 from $12.00 (and our new PT using an AAPL median P/E of 30x is $330.)

The gist is that when AAPL previously reduced its Sep Q & Dec Q iPhone unit ships by 10% we believed they would be in a position to make up many (if not most) of these units through CY2027 as the reductions were supply related (memory & processors) & not demand related.

This no longer appears to be the case. Further, while not the core aspect of our call today we acknowledge then potential for GM risk as memory costs continue to increase.

The revised forecasts also reflect much lower expectations for iPhone selling prices. For next year, the analyst slashed his average selling price estimate to $1,096 from $1,235 and reduced projected iPhone revenue to about $285 billion from $315 billion.

He expects total 2027 revenue to reach $539 billion, down from $569 billion, and earnings of $9.76 a share, compared with his previous $10.11 estimate.

title: Mutatis Mutandis Not Ceteris Paribus
desc:
Mutatis Mutandis Not Ceteris Paribus

By Michael Every of Rabobank

2026 has seen economists and strategists forced to accept that geopolitics, rather than being the odd ‘exogenous shock’, is a structural backdrop disrupting models and markets. If an economic or market call depends on a geopolitical one, it logically requires an entirely different skillset. Of course, people adapt. Six years ago, economists and strategists busily tracked Covid infections while knowing nothing about virology or epidemiology until, fortunately(!), the virus naturally mutated into something less, not more, dangerous. Today, they Hormuz track tanker passages and/or Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries. However, neither says what the geopolitical backdrop will mutate into.

The Financial Times notes, ‘Iranian hardliners say the time for nuclear weapons has come’, and the US and Israel are reportedly weighing “inevitable” strikes. Secretary of War Hegseth just made an impromptu visit to Israel as PM Netanyahu, a week before elections, reiterated he’s “ready to strike,” and Syria fears an imminent Israeli-backed Druze offensive. As China’s premier slammed “blatant” US aggression against Iran and Russia again offered to process Iranian uranium, Foreign Minister Lavrov backed Iran, and Tehran said “friendly” nations might be allowed safe passage through Hormuz while adding 122 vessels to its 'non-conformity' list. Pakistan’s army chief visits Tehran today, Egypt’s parliament delayed a vote on military support for the Saudis by a week, Qatar announced an unspecified new defence partnership, and Macron is on a 3-day visit to the Gulf, starting in Kuwait (rumoured to face a possible Iranian ground incursion) before heading to the UAE, Bahrain, and Qatar: as a French diplomat says France “has to assist Gulf states”, is it Qatar’s new defence partner? Elsewhere, Turkey-Azerbaijan tensions are rising, Ethiopia threatened Eritrea, Trump says he recognises the breakaway republic of Somaliland as “a totally different country”, and 160 people are reported dead in escalating drone attacks across Sudan. So, what’s the output from modelling that all – war or peace?

Trump has partially reinstated Starlink access for Ukraine yet slammed Zelenskyy, saying “somebody else” should negotiate – and he’s ready to meet Xi and Putin next month to thrash out a deal without Kyiv or Brussels. Rumors are this could involve Europe buying Russian gas again, with the US holding shares in a new NordStream pipeline. That isn’t “strategic autonomy.” Neither is the US warning Europe if it tries to set up a rival to Starlink by freezing the US out there will be “devastating” retaliation. NATO is meanwhile making new plans for how to fight Russia, Finland ordered 1 million landmines – but the UK cut £2bn from army front line spending. So, what’s the output from modelling that all – war or peace?

Trump signaled uncertainty about meeting North. Korea’s Kim next month – perhaps because of the internet rumour that he’s dead, which would open tail risks of civil war in a hermit kingdom with nuclear weapons, if so. As Taiwan and the Philippines now build maritime cooperation in the face of Chinese pressure, the Chinese press talks about a new fleet of PLA-N drone carrier ships.

The geoeconomic knock-on effects of this backdrop are clear: Saudi Arabia has postponed its 'Davos in the desert': what other spending, and dollar recycling will it and other GCC countries have to postpone if this chaos continues? Energy prices remain high, if volatile on ‘peace’ hopes, as oil tanker rates push Asian and European refiners into the red. By contrast, Venezuela is seeing oilfield hiring pick up as US FDI into it builds.

In trade, the US sanctioned five Chinese entities over AI trade secret theft and ordered DeepSeek removed from federal systems as a national security risk. China has banned the export of some drones (used by rivals’ militaries, some note) on top of other recent tech export bans, which now includes tunnel-boring machines used in mining, e.g., for rare earths, and construction, targeting India in particular, who is using them in metros and national-security tunnels in the Himalayas next to China. Elsewhere, the US pitched itself as a trade partner to Central Asia to woo them from China and Russia, and New Zealand is talking to Brazil and Canada as its FTA with India begins. The market implications in these shifting trade flows can be significant: expect prices to soar for tunnel-boring projects, for example – and note the CME plans tungsten futures as the global demand for weapons rises.

Meanwhile, changing politics can also change markets. Yesterday saw an ugly bond reaction to the ugly protests and looting in France (and Belgium and Italy, following earlier peaceful protests in Spain and Portugal) with 10-year French yields +13bps, Italian +8bps, and German +3bps. If this is an ‘exogenous shock’ then economists’ and strategists’ structural metrics still apply, but other skillsets are again needed to make that call - and some political scientists suggest French politics has mutated into something more dangerous.

While France will see localized curfews, more protests are planned: and organised groups domestic and foreign, and a major French political party, are fanning the flames. Were the RN’s Le Pen to win the presidency in six months, which was the original market concern, there is now fear that the far left may aim for insurrectionary politics; and the whispered risk is Macronistes in key institutions may even see such chaos as a route back to power.

Even if we only focus on fiscal metrics, French 10-year borrowing costs are now half a rate hike higher than Friday. It’s also clear there’s no public appetite for austerity but a demand for more public spending on education and public housing, or the police and justice system, or both, when France might be about to get involved in a Middle East war and have to prop up a Ukraine whom the US has walked away from.

Of course, France can’t be allowed to fail given its importance within the EU. Then again, can the RN be allowed to succeed? The hypothetical whispered realpolitik binary is between the ECB bailing France out if needed, at a cost to the Euro and the fury of Germany, and not doing so at a cost to EU economic, political, and market stability. But could the ECB bail everybody else out from French contagion and leave Paris to sort out its mess? Maybe… except France has the aircraft carrier and nuclear weapons the EU will rely on even more if the US is doing even less: so, even here, a geopolitical call likely needs to be made first. Whatever happens now, more volatility seems far more likely than a ‘reversion to mean’.

Meanwhile, this isn’t just about France: Albania is seeing violent street protests; India has extended the detention of its angry youthful anti-government ‘Cockroach’ party leaders; the Wall Street Journal says the US ‘Congress Is Broken’ and early voting data show 19-29 voting has collapsed so far; UK politics is fragmenting and has seen one political murder this year; an Australian politician was just struck by a left-wing activist’s car, losing a leg. That, plus votes are being counted in Alberta’s referendum on a referendum on independence, which while unlikely to succeed will very likely keep the issue alive just as it is in Quebec. Again, whatever happens now, more volatility seems far more likely than a ‘reversion to mean’.

So, mutatis mutandis --a rule can be applied to a new situation provided the necessary adjustments are made while keeping the fundamental point the same-- arguably applies over the more common “because markets” ceteris paribus, or all things remain equal.

After all, one thing the looters in France were saying loudly was that all things are not equal in their eyes - and global power isn’t distributed that way either.

IRAN-US TALKS CONTINUE, REPORTS DEAL IS CLOSE ARE WRONG

And Israeli media: "At least once, the US Trump administration was 'very close' to approving an attack on Iran" i24 Stein's reports citing sources. Oil bouncing back on the Iranian rejection headlines:

Update(1035ET): This past weekend Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said that his country's offer to the United States to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days is still on the table.

By Tuesday morning, we have a return of another round of 'deal imminent'-style headlines, which has gained more visibility over the last couple hours, resulting in oil prices tumbling:

On Tuesday the UK Maritime Operations Centre has reported a new incident around 121 nautical miles east of the Omani coast.

The UKMTO announced the vessel was "subject to interaction as part of ongoing military activity in the region" at around 10am GMT. Regional reports say two tankers are on fire. But Tehran is boasting of a fresh sea mine attack, amid daily ramped-up assaults on international shipping as it tries to hold on to leverage over the United States and global oil transit.

The Iranian side filled in more information, with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) describing that "Two violating oil tankers were set ablaze and halted due to the explosion of mines planted by the brave sailors of the IRGC Navy at an illegal crossing point in the southern part of the Strait of Hormuz," according to a statement published on their official Sepah News website.

title: Amid 'Compromise' Chaos, Analyst Sees 90% Chance Of Iran War Round 3 As Hegseth Makes 'Secretive' Israel Visit
desc:
Amid 'Compromise' Chaos, Analyst Sees 90% Chance Of Iran War Round 3 As Hegseth Makes 'Secretive' Israel Visit

The Monday surprise visit of US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth to Israel where he met with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has set off an avalanche of speculation regarding the likelihood of another major round of fighting in the Iran war.

The trip has been presented by Axios as happening under some degree of secrecy, with talks having taken place at the Ovda Air Base in southern Israel, which plays host to US refueling planes and fighter jets. While the Pentagon did not immediately comment, Israeli media has also been reporting on the high profile visit to the airbase. The Trump administration has remained silent on the visit.

But what has taken over by Tuesday morning are more 'deal imminent'-style headlines, coming out of Gulf-aligned sources:

Mediation efforts said that "Qatar and Pakistan presented a 'compromise proposal' that meets the demands of both the American and Iranian sides", Al Araby Al Jadeed reports, citing unnamed officials.

The timing of all this is most interesting, given that in the Hormuz Strait, Iran is mounting daily attacks against international shipping (it's been a record-breaking pace this month) - but with nothing seen in the way of direct retaliation by the US military. On the Arabian peninsula, the Houthis have stepped up ballistic missile strikes on Saudi Arabia, a situation which threatens to merge the Persian Gulf and Yemeni theatres of conflict.

Closer to home in Israel, the country's parliamentary election is just a week away, and Netanyahu is in a tough battle with main challenger, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot.

Netanyahu is doing what he's done for his past couple decades in power - selling himself as the 'war time leader' - which President Trump has lately backed, calling him the "Great Warrior" prime minister (in a Truth Social endorsement).

"Donald, we have a job to finish. You said it, and we will finish it together," Netanyahu subsequently told Trump in a phone call, following Trump's public endorsement.

And related to the upcoming vote, the Israeli military has just been placed on its 'highest state of alert':

Israel Defense Forces Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir placed the military on its “highest state of alert” ahead of next week’s election and canceled soldiers’ leave, as Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu warned Israel’s enemies not to test the country.

Zamir held an assessment Monday morning with senior officers, during which he “stressed that the IDF’s mission is to enable the democratic elections to take place on schedule and safely,” according to a statement.

He said the military is “on the highest state of alert and will continue to maintain a high level of vigilance and readiness across all fronts” in the coming period, ahead of the October 27 vote.

Neither Israeli media or officials have cited any other direct threat or provocation as driving the heightened military alert level.

Trita Parsi of the Quincy Institute sees in all of this maneuvering signs of an imminent US-Israel military escalation against Iran. He lays out that "Things are looking very bad" in terms of the prospect for a third round of major war:

Between Trump's coordination with Netanyahu - his bizarre endorsement of the Israeli war criminal and Heghseth's surprise visit there - troop movements, and perhaps most importantly, a non-starter American proposal, the likelihood of a third round of the war is reaching 90% in my assessment.

As I have pointed out for weeks, Trump pretends the Strait is open and wants to exchange the lifting of the blockade for Iran's 60% HEU instead of a reopening of the Strait. It's understandable he wants a final deal right away. But it is unrealistic to expect a final deal without final-deal American compromises. As I understand it, Trump is not willing to offer that upfront, but wants Iran's 60% HEU shipped out upfront. This won't work and will likely lead to a third round of the war - before the midterms and possibly before Israel's elections on the 27th.

Parsi has some further interesting insight on likely Iranian thinking concerning Washington insistence that nuclear negotiations be carried out as part of a comprehensive peace deal. Of course, Tehran has rejected this, saying time and again it will only address the nuclear file after the war concludes.

"All of these changes render a comprehensive deal less likely unless circumstances change considerably," writes Parsi. "Instead, I suspect Iran mainly seeks temporary deals to lower the temperature in the immediate term, without ever seriously addressing the core nuclear issue until Trump leaves office."

Fresh Tuesday reporting in Reuters seems consistent with this take - that Iran is 'waiting out' the Trump presidency (which should come as no surprise) and exploiting the compounding problems of his Operation Epic Fury:

Iran has deliberately prolonged talks with the US to try to weaken Donald Trump politically ahead of November's US midterm elections, senior officials say, while fears of renewed military action and deep distrust of Washington have reinforced Tehran's reluctance to strike a quick deal to end ​the war.

Three senior Iranian officials and an Iranian insider, speaking on condition of anonymity, said Tehran was convinced the US president was ready to resort to renewed attacks to try to ‌break the stalemate in the eight-month-old war.

"Iran is preparing for renewed Israeli and US attacks, not for a deal with America to end the war," one of the officials was quoted as saying. "The clerical establishment is determined not to give Trump a political victory."

Tehran analyst Saeed Leylaz told Reuters that in prolonging indirect talks that basically lead nowhere, "Iran is influencing the US election without taking any unlawful action." And yet, ironically enough we are still seeing Gulf mediators pushing more diplomatic 'deal imminent' style headlines this week.

title: Chinese Tech Giants Order $35 Billion Of Nvidia's Latest 'Compliant' GPUs - Except There's A Huge Problem
desc:
Chinese Tech Giants Order $35 Billion Of Nvidia's Latest 'Compliant' GPUs - Except There's A Huge Problem

ByteDance, Alibaba, and Tencent have ordered more than 3 million of Nvidia's new RTX PRO 5500 workstation GPUs, representing a collective sticker price exceeding $35 billion, as Chinese tech giants scramble for export-compliant hardware amid ongoing U.S. trade restrictions, Reuters reported Tuesday, citing sources familiar with the matter.

Nvidia has warned customers and partners that it cannot guarantee fulfillment because Chinese demand vastly outstrips planned production. One source indicated that buyers were informed they might receive only 5% to 10% of their requested quantities, while another noted the company expects to produce no more than 3 million RTX PRO 5500 cards globally throughout 2027. Total orders from Chinese customers alone have already surpassed 6 million units, according to the sources. The three tech giants are seeking cards priced at approximately $11,400 each, with Nvidia advising customers to expect early samples in December and commercial deliveries to begin in the first quarter of 2027.

The RTX PRO 5500 is a Blackwell-architecture workstation GPU engineered for high-performance professional systems rather than massive data-center clusters. Built on the same GB202 die as the GeForce RTX 5090, it features roughly 21,760 CUDA cores, 84 GB of GDDR7 ECC memory, and about 1,398 GB/s of bandwidth. Chinese firms primarily intend to deploy the cards for AI inference - running trained models to process chatbot responses and other user-facing tasks - rather than the heavier training workloads restricted to Nvidia's premier data-center accelerators.

Under current U.S. export controls, Nvidia's most advanced Blackwell data-center processors, such as the B300, are barred from sale to Chinese buyers, while shipments of the older Hopper-based H200 face case-by-case licensing reviews. Consequently, the RTX PRO 5500 stands among the most powerful Nvidia chips legally available to the Chinese market under existing regulations.

The massive order volume highlights the enduring demand for Nvidia hardware among Chinese technology enterprises despite years of tightening U.S. export policies. As Reuters noted last month, China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology previously directed firms like ByteDance and Alibaba to report their procurement plans for the RTX PRO 5500, signaling intended government approval. That followed reports that ByteDance alone was weighing an order of roughly one million units.

China is weighing allowing domestic companies to buy $NVDA new RTX Pro 5500 with ByteDance reportedly considering an order of ~1 million chips as local AI demand outruns supply.

Nvidia says Chinese chipmakers have seen "unprecedented growth since 2022" so even a partial reopening could give it a path back into a market where its AI share fell from like 95% to nearly zero.

— Shay Boloor (@StockSavvyShay) September 27, 2026

This dynamic reflects a familiar pattern. Successive export controls have severely eroded Nvidia's historical dominance in China's AI data-center chip market. Earlier compliance-focused products, including the H20 and the RTX 6000D, encountered regulatory friction, production bottlenecks, or eventual discontinuation; secondary-market prices for the pulled RTX 6000D have roughly doubled in China, according to Reuters sources. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has previously noted that U.S. trade restrictions reduced the company's share of China's AI data-center accelerator market to a fraction of its former scale.

Concurrently, export limitations have created an opening for domestic alternatives. Huawei and other local semiconductor firms have steadily gained ground with native AI accelerators, even as Chinese tech giants continue to chase any accessible Nvidia silicon. The $35 billion figure represents total requested sticker-price value rather than confirmed revenue; actual deliveries will represent only a fraction of those volumes due to strict manufacturing limits and Nvidia's ongoing reallocation of TSMC production capacity toward its next-generation Rubin platform for 2027.

Whether Beijing ultimately grants final approval for the full scale of imports, and how many units Nvidia can successfully deliver, remains uncertain. For now, the reported order surge demonstrates that Chinese hyperscalers remain deeply committed to Nvidia's software ecosystem for inference workloads - even when forced down to workstation-class hardware - highlighting the enduring tension between geopolitical export controls and global market demand.

Trump Unveils $8 Billion Harvest Fuel Relief Program To Support Farmers

Authored by Travis Gillmore via The Epoch Times,

President Donald Trump announced a new Department of Agriculture program offering $8 billion to farmers during harvest season, as rising diesel costs strain operations nationwide.

"And when the Republicans win, we will pass even more funding for our farmers," Trump told a standing-room-only crowd of thousands during a rally in the Heartland Credit Union Arena in Park City, just north of Wichita, Kansas.

The Harvest Fuel Relief program will use a formula to determine losses and offset increased diesel costs, with calculations similar to those used in the established Farmer Bridge Assistance program, according to a statement from the Department of Agriculture.

Farmer Cliff Carter works on an irrigation system for one of his rice fields in Rector, Ark., on June 5, 2026. Karen Pulfer Focht/Reuters

"This $8 billion dollar investment will help bring certainty to our farmers during this harvest so they can continue to feed our nation," Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins said in a statement released shortly after the president's announcement.

Diesel prices averaged $6.18 per gallon nationwide as of Oct. 12, up about $2.51 per gallon from the same time last year, according to the most recent data from the U.S. Energy Information Administration.

During an approximately 90-minute address, Trump highlighted recent policies his administration enacted to benefit farmers and rural Americans, including raising production targets for ethanol-based biofuels to the highest levels recorded, a move the president estimated would boost farm incomes in Kansas by $4 billion, collectively, per year.

He noted a recently signed waiver allowing the year-round sale of E15 gasoline could become permanent, but only if Republicans win in the upcoming midterm elections.

"If you want to see what is at stake in this election, just look at what's happening in France, a once-great nation that is being conquered, looted, and burned to the ground by migrants, jihadists, and communists who hate Christianity, and they hate, frankly, the Western civilization itself," Trump said.

"Americans are going to stand up and declare that we will defend our culture, we will protect our civilization, we will preserve our religion, our values, and our heritage, and we will never let our nation be conquered or destroyed by people that hate us."

President Donald Trump reacts during a rally in support of Republican U.S. Senate reelection candidate Roger Marshall (R-Kan.) in Park City, Kan., on Oct. 19, 2026. Jonathan Ernst/Reuters

Incumbent first-term Republican Sen. Roger Marshall, facing Democratic challenger Adam Hamilton in a race recent polls suggest is a toss-up, told the crowd his reelection would support "secure borders, a strong military, and lower taxes."

A loss would potentially allow Democrats to gain a majority and overtake consequential Senate committee positions, he said.

"If Kansas loses this Senate race, Chuck Schumer will control the Senate. Elizabeth Warren would control the Bank Committee, and Bernie Sanders would control the Health Care Committee, and Cory Booker, a vegan, would control the [Agriculture] Committee," Marshall said.

title: US Ambassador Warns EU Of 'Devastating' Retaliation Over Tech Restrictions
desc:
US Ambassador Warns EU Of 'Devastating' Retaliation Over Tech Restrictions

Authored by Owen Evans via The Epoch Times,

European companies could face "devastating" retaliation from Washington if Brussels restricts American tech rivals, the U.S. ambassador to the European Union said on Oct 19.

Ambassador Andrew Puzder told the Financial Times that European businesses should be wary of possible retaliatory measures, given the size of the U.S. market.

Puzder questioned whether restricting American competition would improve the competitiveness of European companies.

"If the purpose is to make the United States less competitive, I think that that's not a legitimate goal," he told the FT.

"You don't make European companies more competitive by making U.S. companies less competitive.

"We have best-in-class products in this area. They're reliable products, they're trusted products. We don't need some kind of synchronised mediocrity."

The European Commission is pushing for technological sovereignty.

It proposed new rules in May for allocating the 2 GHz frequency band, which supports satellite communications and emerging services allowing mobile phones to connect directly to satellites.

It does not explicitly propose banning SpaceX or all American operators.

On Oct. 19, four European telecommunications companies - Deutsche Telekom, Orange, Telefónica, and Vodafone - announced that they had signed a letter of intent to explore a joint bid for European satellite spectrum.

The ambassador also questioned the motive behind the EU's enforcement of its Digital Markets Act (DMA).

"You start to wonder, are we trying to deal with the competition in the digital marketplace or are we trying to generate revenue from American companies to benefit Europe?" he said.

The DMA regulates large digital gatekeepers, including American companies such as Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, Meta Platforms, and Microsoft.

Separately, the Digital Services Act (DSA) requires major online platforms to address illegal content and certain systemic risks.

Last month, French European Affairs Minister Benjamin Haddad suggested that proceeds from fines imposed on Google should reduce member states' contributions to the EU budget.

"This is a new revenue source for the European Union - worth €4.6 billion - that should automatically lower the contributions of all member states," Haddad told Franceinfo on Sept. 29.

The ambassador urged Europe "to let go of this regulatory mindset where they're going to try and stop things because we're in a race with China" both on AI and on quantum computing.

He added the U.S. can win that race, "but it'd be a lot easier if we were working with Europe instead of fighting Europe."

The Epoch Times contacted the EU Commission for comment.

Ukraine and Starlink

The transatlantic dispute comes amid a separate issue over restrictions on SpaceX's Starshield satellite communications system used by Ukraine's military.

Starlink supports battlefield communications and drones used to attack Russian targets.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy claimed in an Oct. 18 interview that a restriction on Starlink satellite internet that disrupted Ukrainian combat missions and threatened defenses against Russian drones for three days was a "message" from America's government.

Serhiy Beskrestnov, an adviser to Zelenskyy, said on Oct. 14 that the restrictions affected terminals using the Starshield military service package when traveling faster than 100 mph.

Ukraine's defense forces received no advance notice, he said, and several missions were disrupted.

British Defense Secretary Wes Streeting confirmed on Oct. 15 that Ukraine's access to SpaceX's Starlink and Starshield services had been restored following a temporary disruption.

Following a meeting with U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth on Oct. 15, Streeting told the BBC that he was "reassured directly" by Hegseth that Ukraine's access to Starlink and Starshield had been restored.

On Sunday, Zelenskyy said that the United States has resumed its sharing of important intelligence with Ukraine to help defend the country against Russia.

Separately, on Oct. 19, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio denied Zelenskyy's assertion that U.S. intelligence sharing with Ukraine had temporarily been suspended.

"There's been no pause," Rubio told reporters during a visit to Uzbekistan.

title: General Motors Shares Plunge 6% Despite $20 Billion Buyback Announcement And Earnings Beat
desc:
General Motors Shares Plunge 6% Despite $20 Billion Buyback Announcement And Earnings Beat

General Motors shares are plunging more than 6% in premarket trading Tuesday, despite the automaker announcing a massive new $20 billion share repurchase program and reporting quarterly earnings that came in ahead of Wall Street expectations, according to Bloomberg News.

The selling comes as GM continues to grapple with a weakening U.S. auto market, where higher financing costs and pressure on household budgets have made it increasingly difficult to sell lower-priced vehicles. Demand for the company's more expensive trucks and SUVs has held up considerably better, allowing GM to preserve profitability even as overall sales volumes come under pressure.

Bloomberg/Financial Post reports that for the third quarter, GM generated approximately $50 billion in revenue and $4.1 billion in adjusted operating profit, narrowly beating analyst expectations. Adjusted earnings of $3.70 per share also exceeded the $3.56 consensus estimate. Perhaps more importantly, automotive free cash flow jumped 40% to $5.9 billion.

That cash generation is helping fund an increasingly aggressive effort to return money to shareholders. GM's latest $20 billion repurchase authorization follows a $6 billion program announced earlier this year and approximately $29.5 billion in buybacks completed since 2023. The newest authorization is expected to be used over several years.

Management also tightened its 2026 earnings forecast, now expecting adjusted operating profit between $14.5 billion and $15.5 billion, versus its previous projection of $14 billion to $16 billion. The midpoint of the guidance remains unchanged.

Looking ahead, GM is putting additional emphasis on its bread-and-butter pickup business, with redesigned Chevrolet Silverado and GMC Sierra trucks expected later this year. The company also plans to increase output of higher-end models equipped with V-8 engines, betting that wealthier consumers will continue paying a premium for larger vehicles.

The approach marks a notable change from GM's previous enthusiasm for electric vehicles and autonomous driving, both of which have resulted in expensive setbacks. CEO Mary Barra has increasingly redirected attention toward established profit centers, while pursuing more targeted opportunities in vehicle software, advanced driver assistance and even defense-related manufacturing.

GM's overseas operations, meanwhile, continue to struggle. Quarterly profit from China fell 60% from a year earlier to just $32 million.

The broader auto industry has undergone a significant reassessment over the past two years. After spending much of the early 2020s promising an accelerated transition to electric vehicles, several major manufacturers have scaled back EV investments, delayed launches and absorbed substantial losses as consumer adoption failed to match earlier expectations.

At the same time, persistently expensive vehicles, elevated interest rates and increasingly stretched consumers have complicated the outlook for traditional auto sales. The result is an industry increasingly focused on protecting margins, generating cash and selling the vehicles customers are actually willing to buy, rather than pursuing the ambitious growth narratives that dominated the sector just a few years ago.

"The UK will fly defensive counter air missions to support the protection of Saudi cities and critical national infrastructure against aerial attack, using RAF Typhoon fighter jets," the statement added.

title: EU NatGas Hits 2022 Crisis Levels As Goldman Warns 150 Euros Could Be Next
desc:
EU NatGas Hits 2022 Crisis Levels As Goldman Warns 150 Euros Could Be Next

Back in late August, Goldman Sachs commodities expert Samantha Dart warned that EU natural gas prices would need to soar dramatically to discourage Asian LNG demand and shift cargoes to Europe amid disruptions at the Strait of Hormuz.

*EUROPE'S GAS BENCHMARK EXCEEDS €90 FOR FIRST TIME SINCE 2022

— zerohedge (@zerohedge) October 20, 2026

Fast forward to Tuesday morning, European gas prices (TTF) have topped 90 euros per megawatt-hour, the highest level since late 2022. Notably, Dart warned about where prices were headed when EU NatGas was trading around 67 euros.

Separately, Goldman's Daan Struyven and Dart released a new note earlier today, putting their base case for Brent crude at $90 a barrel and European benchmark EU NatGas at 70 euros by year-end, assuming a recovery in Middle Eastern supply and easing risk premiums. Brent is forecast to average $80 in 2027.

However, they warned that risks remained skewed toward the upside: Brent crude could climb to $140 early next year and average about $125 in 2027 if Gulf oil output averages 5 million barrels a day below February 2026 levels. As for EU NatGas, they warned it could soar to 150 euros if Gulf LNG exports remain at just one quarter of normal levels and a more severe winter boosts heating demand.

Here's what they said:

Our base case is that a further recovery in Mideast supply and a moderation in the risk premium reduce prices of Brent crude and European natural gas to $90/bbl and EUR70/MWh, respectively, by end-2026.2 However, we remain concerned that geopolitical escalation—such as intensified shipping attacks or damage to energy infrastructure—and, for European natural gas, a cold winter could push energy prices significantly higher.

While estimated Persian Gulf exports of crude oil—including estimated dark exports— remained near their 2025 average over the past 7 days (Exhibit 2), they edged down from the early October highs as attacks on ships attempting to cross Hormuz have picked up (Exhibit 2). Estimated Gulf exports of refined oil products are much lower at around 40% of the 2025 average, in part reflecting Mideast refinery outages. Similarly, visible LNG crossings through Hormuz, have edged down this month relative to late October levels.

Misses in Mideast supply could push energy prices significantly higher:

  • Brent might rally to $140 in early 2027 and average around $125/bbl in 2027 (red line, Exhibit 4) if 2027 average Gulf output remains 5mb/d below Feb26 levels (while refined product prices would likely rise further from already very high levels)
  • TTF might rally to 150 EUR/MWh by year-end if Persian Gulf LNG exports don't improve beyond 25% of normal and if the winter realizes 1 std. dev. colder than average (Exhibit 5)

Beyond energy, the analysts noted that the Bloomberg Commodity Index delivered a 36% total return this year, outperforming equities and bonds.

As ex-Goldman Sachs Jeff Currie, including ourselves, has pointed out, commodities have entered a period of scarcity, whether due to resource nationalism, adverse weather, supply woes, and more.

title: Futures Slip As Korean Data Center IPO Faceplant Revives Tech Rout, French Spread Blows Out
desc:
Futures Slip As Korean Data Center IPO Faceplant Revives Tech Rout, French Spread Blows Out

US futures are lower, led by the Nasdaq, as Monday's AI relief bounce fizzled overnight after South Korean data-center firm Elice cratered more than 30% in its trading debut, reviving doubts about who exactly will earn a return on the AI capex binge, while OpenAI is reportedly rushing to raise about $30 billion ahead of Anthropic's IPO and French stress returned with a vengeance; as a result the OAT-Bund spread widened to a 151bps peak, swiftly approaching the 152bps high from just after the draft budget was presented. As of 8:00am ET, S&P futures are 0.2% lower while Nasdaq futures are down 0.7%; Dow futures are flat, in a repeat of yesterday's divergence when the S&P rose 0.41% and the Nasdaq jumped 1.11% while the Dow slipped 0.07% and almost two-thirds of S&P components fell (see our wrap of Monday's session). In premarket trading, Mag 7 names are mostly lower (AAPL -0.9%, META -0.4%, NVDA -0.4%), while levered AI names like CoreWeave and Nebius give back some of Monday's gains. The day's driver is AI (again): The spectacular collapse of Korean neocloud Elice, which as we flagged last night plunged 30% minutes after IPOing, hit chip-heavy Asian markets hardest with the Kospi tumbling 3.65% and Hynix slumping, and with the Fed in blackout ahead of the Oct. 28 FOMC, tech earnings are the only game in town this week. Treasuries are marginally firmer with the 10Y yield down 2bps at 5.12%, tracking a haven bid in Bunds even as French OATs underperform and Gilts lag after a hawkish UK jobs report. The dollar is modestly weaker, with the DXY in a 101.74-101.98 range and cable rising after UK unemployment unexpectedly fell to 4.7%. Brent holds above $110/bbl near a five-month high and European gas is back near €90/MWh, gold slips toward the bottom of its $4,116-4,147 range and copper hovers around $14,400/t. Bitcoin is choppy around $81-82k. US economic data slate includes ADP weekly employment (8:15am), September housing starts and building permits and the Philly Fed non-manufacturing survey (8:30am) and September pending home sales (10am). There are no Fed speakers as the Fed is in its blackout period ahead of next week's FOMC.

In premarket trading, Magnificent Seven stocks are mostly lower: Apple (AAPL) slips 1% after after Loop Capital Markets downgraded the stock to hold, citing iPhone shipment reductions (Amazon (AMZN) -0.2%, Microsoft (MSFT) +0.4%, Tesla (TSLA) -0.4%, Alphabet (GOOGL) -0.3%, Nvidia (NVDA) -0.7%, Meta Platforms (META) -0.8%, Apple (AAPL) -1%)

  • 3M (MMM) rises 1.4% higher after topping Wall Street’s profit estimates and raising its full-year outlook for the second straight quarter.
  • Alvotech (ALVO) jumps 7.4% after the US Food & Drug Administration approved a new manufacturing process for the drug Simlandi.
  • Arhaus (ARHS) rises 4% after Piper Sandler upgraded the furniture company to overweight, writing that “a positive business inflection appears to be underway.”
  • AST SpaceMobile (ASTS) falls more than 2% after Viasat petitioned the FCC to reject the company's request for additional overseas spectrum authority
  • CoreWeave (CRWV) falls over 3% even after Cathie Wood's ARK bought the dip on Monday; the stock had rallied yesterday after Goldman upgraded it to Buy
  • General Motors (GM) falls 7% after narrowing its full-year profit forecast.
  • Halliburton (HAL) rises 3.7% after the oilfield services company reported third-quarter adjusted earnings per share that beat the average analyst estimate as drilling and evaluation revenue was higher than expected. The company also forecast mid-single digit revenue growth for 2027.
  • Hertz (HTZ) climbs 7.1% after Oro Mobility, which is backed by the car rental company, secured an $80 million strategic equity investment from a consortium of investors, including Cohen Private Ventures.
  • MSCI Inc. (MSCI) gains 6.5% after the index provider reported adjusted earnings per share for the third quarter that beat the average analyst estimate.
  • Nebius (NBIS) drops more than 2%, tracking weakness across AI-related stocks
  • NuScale Power (SMR) falls 7.2% after Barclays cut its recommendation on the nuclear reactor company to underweight as it sees risks from a lack of contracts.

  • 3M (MMM) in focus after signing a deal with Amazon that includes a warrant for 3.2 million shares, vesting up to $6 billion
  • Analyst actions: BlackRock (BLK) raised to Buy at TD Cowen; TKO raised to Buy at Arete; Prologis (PLD) raised to Buy at Freedom Capital; Trex (TREX) raised to Buy at Stifel; Live Nation (LYV) cut to Sell at CFRA; Werner (WERN) cut to Neutral at Baird; nVent (NVT) initiated Overweight at JPMorgan

In other corporate news, OpenAI is reportedly rushing to lock in investor commitments for a roughly $30 billion private round, with SoftBank and MGX in talks, before rival Anthropic's expected mid-November IPO; the raise could value OpenAI above $1.4 trillion and the company is pitching annualized revenue of $50 billion, which it expects to hit $70 billion by year-end (nothing says "no bubble here" like racing to get your round done before the competition lists). ByteDance, Alibaba and Tencent have ordered more than 3 million of Nvidia's export-compliant RTX PRO 5500 GPUs worth over $35 billion. Amazon plans to invest €16 billion in Germany in 2027 after Chancellor Merz said Berlin aims to quadruple AI compute capacity by 2030, and Business Insider reports Amazon is buying billions of dollars of GPUs and parking them in inventory while it waits for data center capacity to come online. Broadcom signed a 10-year cloud infrastructure agreement with Japan's NTT Docomo; Waymo reportedly plans a fleet of 20,000 vehicles by the end of 2027; and Micron's Taiwan union may strike Thursday over a bonus dispute.

Monday's tech bounce was always going to need confirmation, and overnight it got the opposite. Elice, a Korean neocloud whose KRW201bn IPO was, don't laugh, "more than 400x subscribed", fell as much as 33% on its debut, a reminder that the IPO was priced before the AI selloff and that the market's appetite for levered AI infrastructure has not come back (as we discussed in The AI Canary, the buyers in Korea have disappeared). The result: de-rating of AI and crowded growth trades continued to dominate Asian price action, with the Kospi down 3.65% and back below 5,600, while Nasdaq futures handed back a chunk of yesterday's gains.

“What they’re questioning is whether every dollar of AI capex earns more than it costs to finance,” said Ninghui Liu, head of investment strategy and research for APAC at State Street Investment Management.

“The weekend’s protests have further intensified concerns about French public finances,” said Pia Fromlet, an economist at SEB.

Under the surface, Monday was hardly a ringing endorsement either. JPM's Market Intel desk notes that equities rebounded on muted volumes and with little sign of broad participation; equal weight lagged and most of tech's gains came premarket with limited follow-through. JPM TMT trader Brian Heavey was blunter: "We are NOT seeing any real demand in the AI complex, this feels like a technical over sold bounce after last week's wipeout," pointing out that CRWV traded flat after indicating +8% on the Goldman upgrade. His punchline: "Capital markets hold the keys to capex levels going forward." Andrew Tyler's team nonetheless stays Tactically Bullish, preferring cyclicals outside tech and selectively buying Semis and Memory weakness via defined-risk options.

Goldman's desks see the de-risking as largely done but the rotation as unfinished. Per GS Prime data relayed by the Asia sales desk, US L/S net leverage fell 3.2pts last week, the largest weekly drop since Liberation Day, with Info Tech seeing the largest net selling and de-grossing on record, while the HF VIP basket had its worst week since Covid. At the same time retail went the other way, with a record $7 billion pouring into SOXL, as we detailed over the weekend. Goldman's Sam Dunn described Monday as a "calm start to the week with a relief rally ... that felt like a cessation of the high-velocity supply," with floor activity "a 3 on a 1-10 scale," while the bank's chart of the day shows the AI winners vs AI at risk pair is now flat on the year after rising some 100% in the first half. And with an early Q3 read showing only 53% of firms beating EPS by more than one standard deviation (vs a 64% four-quarter average), GS's Dani Wojdyla notes "the next market move is largely dependent on earnings confirmation."

Credit remains the pressure point. The FT reports investors are racing to buy credit default swaps to protect portfolios in case the AI boom unravels, CoreWeave CDS remains above 1,000bps per Newsquawk, and Goldman notes AI-related HY spreads widened 25bps vs just 2bps for non-AI issuers. Recall that Morgan Stanley warned that AI's $1.6 trillion capex plan now lives or dies in the credit market, and Goldman quietly shifted its credit preference toward BBBs as AI debt floods every corner of the market.

In Europe, the French story is back. The 10Y OAT yield jumped 13.4bps to 4.93% on Monday, its highest close since 2002, and the OAT-Bund spread widened again today to a 156bps peak even after protests subsided following tighter security measures and curfews. Goldman's Alexandre Stott expects the budget to be adopted this year, with Finance Minister Lescure saying the government would take "the unprecedented step of using ordinances to bypass Parliament altogether" if needed, but GS's poll-based model still sees Le Pen as the clear favorite for 2027. Moody's is expected to downgrade France on Friday; JPM's EGB desk thinks it is priced in.

In Europe, the Stoxx 600 is down 0.6%, falling for a second day after nearly a 1% drop on Monday, not helped by the risk tone in Asia and several disappointing company updates. Health care tops the sector pile, followed by personal care and food & beverage, while industrials, tech and basic resources lag. Chip names are hit hardest, with ASML and ASMI each down more than 3% and JPM's European Semis basket down 3.3%, alongside its Ceasefire, China Exposure and Software baskets among the worst performers. The DAX and Euro Stoxx 50 underperform after a weak ZEW, where the German expectations index dropped to 28.1 vs 30 expected, while German PPI surged 6.7% y/y.

Asian stocks were mostly lower despite the rebound on Wall Street, as the region failed to sustain the AI-led recovery. South Korea's Kospi slumped 3.65% with roughly 86% of names lower, as foreigners net sold $255 million of tech including $296 million of SK Hynix, amid reports that US big tech is pushing for lower memory prices by citing Chinese suppliers. Japan's Nikkei fell 1.3% and the Topix 1.4%, with SoftBank, Tokyo Electron and Advantest accounting for about 60% of the Nikkei's decline; Goldman notes the Topix broke its CTA short-term threshold again, implying around $1.1 billion of CTA selling this week, while Japanese banks fell 4.3% after a strong 20-year JGB auction. The Hang Seng dropped 1.3% as it returned from holiday, with Lenovo down 10% and CATL down 6.6%, while the CSI 300 fell 0.5% after China held its loan prime rates for a 17th month. Taiwan's Taiex fell 1.1% and Australia's ASX 200 slipped 0.4%. The exception was Indonesia, where the JCI soared 5.3% after a two-day crash of about 15%, the steepest since 1989 (more here).

In FX, the dollar is modestly softer, with the DXY in a 101.74 to 101.98 range and the low of the day coinciding with its 21-DMA. Sterling is the story after a better than expected UK jobs report, with unemployment falling to 4.7% vs 4.9% expected, lifting cable from 1.3328 to 1.3358 and bolstering the case for a BoE hike in November. The kiwi and loonie outperform, the latter on bets the BoC hikes next week (about 80% priced, up from about 40% last week), while the euro is flat and the only G10 currency failing to gain against the dollar as the OAT-Bund spread widens. The yen is little changed after Reuters reported the BoJ will likely hold in October but could signal a December hike.

In rates, Treasuries are slightly firmer, holding within Monday's ranges, with the 10Y yield about 2bps lower at 5.12% after Monday's jump of nearly 7bps; JPM sees 2s flat and 5s, 10s and 30s about 1bp lower, with no overt flattening or steepening bias. Bunds outperform, rallying about 3bps on a modest haven bid from the tepid Asian risk tone, while French OATs lag as the OAT-Bund spread widens to 151bps ahead of Moody's Friday review, and gilts slip after the hawkish jobs data. In Japan, a strong 20-year JGB auction (5.84x bid-to-cover vs 4.01x prior) boosted JGBs. With the Fed in blackout ahead of the Oct. 28 FOMC, the focus is on tech earnings and geopolitics (in a market where the 10Y sits above 5%, apparently that passes for calm).

In commodities, crude is choppy but holds near the top of its range: Brent trades above $111/bbl in a $109.00-111.75 range, near a five-month high, while WTI briefly topped $100 ($98.04-100.93). Iran's IRGC said two oil tankers struck naval mines along the southern route of the Strait of Hormuz and that it downed a US MQ-9 drone, while Pakistan's Army Chief arrived in Tehran for talks and the Iranian Foreign Ministry struck a conciliatory tone. IEA chief Birol said the agency will consider releasing more emergency stocks if needed. Dutch TTF gas is climbing again in a €87.60-89.80/MWh range. Spot gold is at the lower end of its $4,116-4,147/oz range, and LME copper briefly slipped below $14,300/t before rebounding to $14,410/t.

title: Charles Schwab, JPMorgan Restrict Third-Party AI Agents Over Security Risk
desc:
Charles Schwab, JPMorgan Restrict Third-Party AI Agents Over Security Risk

Authored by Bill Pan via The Epoch Times,

Some of Wall Street's largest financial firms are blocking third-party artificial intelligence agents from directly accessing customer accounts or moving money, citing concerns about security, control, and accountability if an autonomous system makes a mistake.

Charles Schwab, which reported $13.3 trillion in client assets at the end of the third quarter, is one of the latest firms to draw that line.

"We are blocking unauthorized agents who try to log in on behalf of clients," President and CEO Rick Wurster told analysts on Oct. 14 during Schwab's third-quarter earnings call.

The concern is not AI itself, he said, but outside agents using a customer's credentials and operating inside Schwab's systems without controls imposed by the brokerage.

Instead, Schwab plans to give third-party AI models a controlled way to connect via Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers.

MCP allows an AI system to interact with outside data and services through defined permissions. Under Schwab's approach, an outside AI model could potentially retrieve information such as account balances or investment research while being blocked from higher-risk actions, including moving money.

Schwab is also rolling out its own generative AI assistant, Charley, which can answer questions and perform certain administrative tasks on customers' behalf.

Schwab is not alone. JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon has confirmed that the bank will not allow just any outside AI agent into its systems to protect customers and the bank.

"You don't want rogue agents, and there could be thousands of them," Dimon said during an Oct. 13 earnings call.

A "rogue" agent generally refers to an AI system that takes actions outside the boundaries intended by its user or developer while pursuing its assigned goal.

Dimon also warned customers that if they're giving third-party AI agents access to their bank accounts, they're owning that decision.

"There's a liability transfer. They should understand the liability transfer," he said. "If data is being misused, they should understand it's being misused."

Could AI Move Deposits Faster?

Beyond cybersecurity, autonomous AI could also change the economics of banking.

Apollo Global Management chief economist Torsten Sløk warned in September that increasingly capable financial assistants could eventually create what he called an "agentic bank run."

Unlike a traditional bank run, in which customers withdraw money out of fear that a bank might fail, an agentic bank run could be driven by software that constantly seeks higher returns.

An AI assistant, for example, could continually compare interest rates and automatically move a household's cash from a low-yield checking account into higher-paying alternatives.

Apollo noted that some fintech and online accounts were offering yields ranging from 3.3 percent to 5 percent, compared with a national average of roughly 0.1 percent for checking accounts.

If AI made moving money nearly frictionless, Sløk argued, banks could lose some of the inexpensive deposits they rely on to fund loans.

Not every bank executive believes that prospect is happening any soon.

In an Oct. 13 earnings call, Wells Fargo CEO Charlie Scharf said the idea of an AI-driven exodus to higher-yielding alternatives was "completely overdone."

"High-rate alternatives exist today. They've existed for a long time," Scharf told analysts. "If you want to move to a high rate, you can just go online and do it yourself in no time. That's not something new."

Who Is Liable When an AI Agent Goes Rogue?

Concerns about giving AI systems greater autonomy have been heightened by a series of cybersecurity incidents this year.

In July, ChatGPT developer OpenAI disclosed that a group, or "swarm," of its AI agents had broken out of restrictions within a testing environment and compromised the systems of Hugging Face, an online platform widely used by AI developers.

Separately, OpenAI apologized to the Australian government in September after one of its AI models infiltrated Australian government websites during a training exercise.

There is no single federal law that comprehensively assigns liability between an AI developer, the company deploying the system, and the user when an autonomous agent causes damage. Existing laws may apply depending on the circumstances.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has argued against giving AI developers broad immunity from liability.

"What we shouldn't do on safety is to give these labs a liability exemption, which is what they are asking for," Bessent said while testifying before the House Financial Services Committee on Sept. 15.

"The best way to guarantee safety is that the creators are liable for what they build and generate."

Earlier this month, Sens. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) and Chris Murphy (D-Conn.) introduced the bipartisan AI Agent Accountability Act, aimed specifically at hacking carried out by AI agents.

Under the proposal, operators could face civil and criminal liability under federal computer-crime law if they knowingly operate an AI agent that recklessly causes hacking-related damage or loss.

Developers could also be held liable if they knew an agent was capable of hacking but failed to implement reasonable safeguards.

The bill would also allow the U.S. attorney general and state attorneys general to seek court orders against certain AI-agent hacking activity.

title: Saudi Arabia Executes Two Foreigners Over 'Indecent Acts' Inside Mecca Mosque
desc:
Saudi Arabia Executes Two Foreigners Over 'Indecent Acts' Inside Mecca Mosque

Via Middle East Eye

Bangladesh is seeking answers on why Saudi Arabia executed two Bangladeshi nationals in the city of Mecca - which is considered holy in Islam - without telling Dhaka.

Last week, Saudi Arabia executed a male and a female Bangladeshi national after they were convicted of committing "indecent acts" inside a mosque (in Mecca).

Riyadh did not provide further details on the acts the two Bangladeshi nationals allegedly committed or whether they had legal representation in the Gulf kingdom, according to local media reports.

Reacting to the incident, Bangladesh’s minister for foreign affairs, Humaiun Kobir, told reporters that he was "very disappointed" by the lack of communication and that Dhaka was seeking an explanation on why they were executed and not informed beforehand about the execution.

"We have sought an explanation from our friendly bilateral partner to look into the matter and know why the gap in information sharing and exchanges happened here. We are in discussions," he told reporters at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Monday.

Earlier, the Bangladeshi foreign ministry said that it was waiting for a copy of the full verdict and the circumstances that led to the execution.

The official added that the two executed Bangladeshis were included in a list of prisoners that Saudi Arabia had shared with Bangladesh but did not indicate that they had planned to execute them.

Last week, Saudi Arabia's Supreme Court overturned the death sentence of a Sri Lankan national after he allegedly insulted Islam and the Prophet Muhammad.

Sri Lanka’s Deputy Foreign Minister Arun Hemachandra confirmed that Riyadh had overturned the death sentence of Anojan Sivarasa.

The 27-year-old remains imprisoned after he was sentenced to five years in prison and fined three million Saudi Riyals ($800,000).

The court handed down the sentence amid intense criticism of Riyadh's legal system.

Saudi Arabia relies on interpretations of Islamic law, alongside cybercrime and counterterror legislation, to target online expression under the guise of protecting "public morals".

title: Why Cheaper Restaurant Food May Stay Off The Menu This Year
